content:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

title: Jensen Huang and the Myth of Indispensability
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.Jensen Huang said in a statement this morning that he would be “honored” to return to Nvidia, the compu...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Jensen Huang said in a statement this morning that he would be “honored” to return to Nvidia, the computer-chip giant from which he was ousted just last week.

Unfortunately for Huang, the company’s board made it clear on today’s earnings call that it’s not considering rehiring him. But major figures in Silicon Valley have been making a show of their continued support. For another, less powerful executive, reports of extramarital affairs with three women—one of whom is alleged to be a Chinese spy and another of whom was a direct subordinate—would likely be seen as irredeemable lapses in judgment. Yet Huang’s endorsers don’t seem to view this as the end of his career at the company.

“Without Jensen,” Elon Musk claimed on X this weekend, Nvidia will lose important “handshake” deals that Huang personally negotiated. Gavin Baker, whose firm invests in Nvidia, has written that he’s in favor of reinstating Huang as the investigations play out. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney remarked on X that “journalists with sketchy motives” effectively “gaslit” the board into pushing out a “once-in-generation visionary.” An Uber co-founder, Travis Kalanick, who knows a thing or two about tech ousters, was among the more than 195,000 signatories of a petition to reinstate Huang as the company’s CEO—as were Musk, Baker, and Sweeney. The Wall Street Journal reports that a high-level Nvidia employee sent a letter to the company’s board warning that “irreplaceable talent” might leave if Huang isn’t reinstated. When President Trump was asked yesterday whether he’d support the return of Huang, a close ally, he told reporters, “I would not mind that.”

Ultimately, none of these people has full control over Huang’s fate. That power belongs to Nvidia’s board of directors. But the support for Huang, despite his clearly disqualifying transgressions, is a testament to the power that this one man has held over Nvidia and the economy at large. (It may also be informed by the dramatic firing and rehiring of another tech titan: Sam Altman.) Even though Huang is accused of having jeopardized national security, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is now reportedly probing whether Nvidia violated investor-disclosure laws, his backers insist that he remains indispensable. Their argument is that he is the company, and that the risks of losing him might actually outweigh the risks of bringing him back as CEO. In a way, they are right: Huang has made himself synonymous with Nvidia. But his centrality is a liability rather than an asset. This moment should be a reckoning about the risks of relying so heavily on any one CEO—yet many in the industry are reinforcing the opposite lesson, doubling down on a disgraced executive.

Nvidia is what you might call a “systematically important” institution—industry lingo for a company whose failure would destabilize parts of the financial system. Wall Street trembled after the revelations about Huang spurred a roughly $1.5 trillion sell-off in Nvidia stock (equivalent to more than 25 percent of the company’s value). The AI sector, and in turn the entire U.S. economy, is heavily dependent on the firm’s chips. “Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation,” my colleague Charlie Warzel wrote last week. “Huang is too big to fail. Which may be why so many people seem motivated to downplay or protect him right now.”

Some of this is owed to the myth of the tech leader as an irreplaceable genius—a story that Silicon Valley loves to tell. As The Washington Post points out, nearly a tenth of the value of the S&P 500 is tied to companies with no clear successor: Nvidia, Tesla, and Meta. Huang himself liked to boast about his famously flat org structure—he had 60 direct reports. The New York Times notes that Nvidia’s board, which is now investigating whether Huang was the target of Chinese espionage, has a history of “loyalty and deference” to him. Some of its directors have been on the board since 1993.

Public outcry has been an effective tactic in bringing back ousted tech leaders in the past; in late 2023, OpenAI’s board fired Altman because he “was not consistently candid in his communications” with them—but reinstated him five days later after a company-wide revolt. Like Huang, Altman is a celebrity co-founder. He’s the face of his company and the person seen as largely responsible for its success. Any of Altman’s shortcomings or misdeeds were considered secondary to, and distinct from, his ability to generate value for shareholders.

Obviously, this isn’t the first case of an executive facing consequences over a relationship with an employee: McDonald’s fired its CEO over this in 2019, Intel’s CEO resigned in 2018 after failing to disclose a relationship with a subordinate, Boeing pushed out its CEO in 2006 over a similar situation. The ongoing national-security concerns add another layer of urgency to the situation. The question of how much Huang actually knew about Megaspeed—the company that the alleged Chinese spy worked for, which the U.S. Department of Commerce has been looking into since 2024—is currently under investigation. Investors are angry enough that they’re suing Nvidia over the fiasco (the company had initially denied that there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about its CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive until Huang himself admitted to it; Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment).

Not everyone is pushing for Huang’s comeback. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has suggested that he’d like to see Nvidia pick a new CEO from outside the company, and some lawmakers have opposed the idea of Huang’s return. But those who want him reinstated are selling a dangerous narrative about the indispensability of any one leader. The celebrity investor Balaji Srinivasan wrote today that “it’s arguably a matter of US national security to immediately return the most important person in AI to his role at the top AI company”—never mind that Nvidia, under Huang, may have been responsible for allowing the United States’ biggest economic rival to access top-tier computer chips. Tying an entire enterprise to the success or failure of a single person comes with extreme risks; Huang’s defenders are ignoring them.

The United States has lost its measles-elimination status for the first time since 2000, after more than a year of continuous transmission amid declining vaccination rates, the Pan American Health Organization announced.   2. The National Security Agency’s highly classified internal-communications network went down today, prompting staggered employee arrivals as officials investigated the disruption, CNN reported. An Almost Entirely Unregulated Corner of the Health-Care Workforce

By Olga Khazan

When Mariah Stockman went into labor with her first child, her husband called their doula and told her to come to the hospital right away. Despite the urgency of the situation, the doula, Stockman said, asked her husband if she had time to stop and get a coffee. Two and a half hours later, the doula walked into Stockman’s delivery room. “I’ll never forget the coffee in her fucking hand,” Stockman told me recently.

Her doula, she said, caught only the last 10 or so minutes of her labor, and she didn’t visit after the baby’s birth, as they had agreed on. Stockman said she paid $2,500 for the doula’s services: “What a waste.”

title: Diplomacy, but Make It Obnoxious
summary: Tyra Banks had a tip for how contestants on America’s Next Top Model should present themselves: “Ho, but make it fashion.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s recent speeches update the message with a twist: “Traditional American foreign policy, but make it obnoxious.” Twice in six weeks, Rubio has del...
content:
Tyra Banks had a tip for how contestants on America’s Next Top Model should present themselves: “Ho, but make it fashion.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s recent speeches update the message with a twist: “Traditional American foreign policy, but make it obnoxious.” Twice in six weeks, Rubio has delivered addresses filled with classic conservative beliefs, but seasoned with the kind of racism, sexism, and enthusiasm for lawless power that has become common in the age of Trump.

At a Federalist Society conference Friday evening, Rubio offered an explanation for the Trump administration’s decision last month to impose sanctions on what he called the “fake” International Criminal Court—a move apparently made in retaliation against the ICC’s investigation of alleged U.S. war crimes in Afghanistan. In making his case, Rubio had two options. The first would have been to point out that every American administration of the past three decades has rejected ICC jurisdiction over U.S. personnel. As president, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden all expressed openness to the ICC—but only if the court accepted some kind of U.S. veto. The case for this option is that it would have created the broadest possible coalition behind the Trump administration’s position. This was the approach George W. Bush’s administration took in the early 2000s, citing Clinton’s qualms about the ICC to support Bush’s stronger stance against the court.

The second option was for Rubio to deliver a message of skepticism about the ICC, but going pedal-to-the-metal culture war. This, unfortunately, was the option Rubio went for. In explaining the administration’s policy toward the ICC, Rubio cited a line attributed to the Roman general Pompey: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth liked the bit so much, he reposted it on X, capping “MEN WITH SWORDS.”

[Read: The dangerous idea Rubio and Hegseth are endorsing]

Watch the video of these remarks, and you’ll hear nervous laughter after Rubio’s Pompey reference. When he noticed that his big applause line had misfired, Rubio flashed an apologetic smile and improvised: “Not politically correct to say that, but that’s what he said!” The attempted regroup extracted more chuckles but scant applause.  

Rubio was speaking to an ultra-friendly room. The majority of the conservative lawyers convened before him surely agreed with his preceding point about the ICC: “They think they have the right to rule over everyone, but they are accountable to no one, armed with the power to investigate, to prosecute, to persecute, and to jail our citizens according to laws we neither consent nor control.” But American lawyers—even conservative ones—will not agree that the capacity to do violence exempts armed men from the law.

We know Pompey’s views on men with swords because they appear in Plutarch’s collection of short biographies of eminent Greeks and Romans. Plutarch’s Pompey is no hero, but a man of great gifts laid low by bad judgment. After the Bible, Plutarch’s Lives ranked high among the books read by America’s Founding Fathers. James Madison, the country’s fourth president and Rubio’s predecessor as secretary of state by more than 215 years, had little good to say about warlords such as Pompey: “The liberties of Rome proved the final victim to her military triumphs.”

Rubio has a reputation as one of the Trump’s administration’s less irresponsible figures. But his approach to rhetoric lately seems borrowed from a story told about Franklin D. Roosevelt by his aide, Raymond Moley. During the presidential campaign of 1932, Moley showed Roosevelt two competing drafts of a big economic speech. One called for junking tariffs. The other endorsed them. Which approach, Moley asked, would the candidate prefer? “Weave the two together,” Roosevelt replied. Rubio likewise sometimes presents himself as the last voice of Republican internationalism, a defender of America’s long history of democratic alliances and partnerships. Other times, he remembers that this music no longer moves his party under Trump—and instead deploys language that is bombastic, vituperative, and needlessly disparaging.

In Rubio’s speech on democracy in Athens last month, for example, he swerved from praising the pursuit of knowledge to delivering an encomium to violent conquest: “The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’s discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon. And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.”

Rubio’s Federalist Society speech was mostly about international law, but it included a completely unnecessary passage that implied that Native Americans are not part of the American “we.” He said, “When our predecessors first arrived in North America, when they first came, there were no factories, there were no railroads, there were no skyscrapers. These things exist because we built them, because we acted. These things exist because we acted without fear or moral doubt and overcame all that which threatened or stood in our way.”

[Read: Trump sets the olive branch on fire]

These speeches deploy gendered language (“the men who founded my country”; “the men who built backwater colonies into the greatest superpower on Earth”; “the men who made the Parthenon”; “the sons of Athens and Rome”) with an emphasis and frequency that must have raised eyebrows even in a Trump-administration communications department. When I wrote speeches for a Republican administration more than a quarter century ago, language that obliviously elided about half of the human race would have earned me a zinger from one of the administration’s many high-ranking women.

For the Cabinet secretary charged with the care of alliances and institutions, such fretting over the mollycoddling do-gooders who are crushing the spirits of the Nietzschean supermen among us is unusual. But in his speech in Greece, Rubio lamented that Western institutions care more for “the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best,” adding: “We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.”

To the Federalist Society, Rubio complained of how “international lawyers and jurists and NGOs and UN bureaucrats” conspire to persuade the United States “to relinquish responsibility for our own destiny and to relieve ourselves of the burdens of greatness and seek refuge in these glittering generalities of international law.” He expressed annoyance that the president “cannot restrict trade or immigration or even examine the way in which we spend our citizens’ tax dollars abroad without facing the fury” of these meddlesome international bodies: “Even as we defeated the institution of Soviet communism, we did not triumph over the spirit of Marx.”

But it was not Karl Marx who struck down Trump’s attempts to exert unilateral presidential authority over trade and immigration. It was America’s own courts—in many cases led by Federalist Society–style judges—that ruled against Trump’s claims that the president can impose tariffs at will and overturn birthright citizenship by executive order.

What’s achieved by these bizarre excursions down such malign byways? The early bidding for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination is shaping up as a contest among Vice President Vance, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, and a widening field that includes Rubio and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas. Like Vance, Rubio has seemed to intuit that the way to prove one’s mettle in a party remade by Trump is to present oneself as gratuitously nasty. But this is an odd gamble at a time when the president’s own gratuitous nastiness has inspired the country’s turn away from him and his party.

title: An Obituary for America’s Measles-Elimination Status
summary: UNITED STATES—A scientific triumph that quietly shaped a generation, the United States’ measles-elimination status passed away on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Hailed as an unmitigated good and a borderline miracle on its initial appearance, then quickly forgotten, Measles Elimination had seemed to ha...
content:
UNITED STATES—A scientific triumph that quietly shaped a generation, the United States’ measles-elimination status passed away on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Hailed as an unmitigated good and a borderline miracle on its initial appearance, then quickly forgotten, Measles Elimination had seemed to have many more good years ahead of it. Its decline was sudden and dramatic, and it had been feuding with the secretary of health and human services for some time, although he denied having any direct role in its demise.

Observers described its death as “senseless,” “utterly senseless,” “an enormous step backward,” and “the kind of thing that makes you lose all hope in human progress.”

Measles Elimination arrived in 2000 as the proud work of scientists and doctors and public messaging. Praised at the time as one of the country’s greatest public-health achievements, it had hoped to make way for many more such eliminations. “Now, instead, we are looking at the first of many obituaries that didn’t need to be written,” one observer commented.

Parents are finding it wrenching to explain to their children that Measles Elimination won’t be around anymore. “I feel so bad that we took the elimination of measles for granted,” one mother said. “We were presenting it to our kids like, Measles Elimination isn’t going anywhere. Measles Elimination will be there long after I’m gone. No part of this is how I hoped I’d be explaining death to them for the first time.”

“Measles Elimination never wanted to be the story,” its old friend and mentor Uncontaminated Food remarked. “It wanted the story to be the other things that it was making possible. I was always telling people: If you’re here, if you’re pursuing your dreams, if your immune system is functioning, if you’re attending school year-round without interruption, you owe that to Measles Elimination. People forgot all the work it was doing.” Uncontaminated Food coughed for an uncomfortably long period of time. “I always thought I would be the first to go. This makes me sick.”

No ceremony will be held; Measles Elimination stated in its will that the last thing it would want would be a large gathering in its honor. It asked for donations to be made in its name to vaccine clinics.

Measles Elimination was only 26—older, though, than many will get to be without it.

title: Trump’s Arch Must Be Stopped
summary: In 1962, my father faced a novel threat to the Constitution. The governor of Mississippi had defied a federal court order and physically blocked a young Black Air Force veteran from attending the University of Mississippi. As U.S. attorney general, my father—Robert F. Kennedy—knew he had to do somet...
content:
In 1962, my father faced a novel threat to the Constitution. The governor of Mississippi had defied a federal court order and physically blocked a young Black Air Force veteran from attending the University of Mississippi. As U.S. attorney general, my father—Robert F. Kennedy—knew he had to do something. The governor was backed by a state police force that acted as his personal militia. There was, and is, no federal police force that my father or his brother, President John F. Kennedy, could deploy to deal with a lawless chief executive at the state level.

My father cobbled together a force of duly deputized U.S. marshals, many of them drawn from the ranks of the U.S. Border Patrol. He sent two courageous Justice Department attorneys—World War II veterans—to prepare the marshals before deploying them to Oxford, Mississippi. They were able, barely, to protect James Meredith on his first day at the university. Eventually, about 30,000 troops and National Guardsmen were activated to protect Meredith.

The lesson my father drew was simple: The Constitution does not enforce itself. When those sworn to uphold the law refuse to do so, someone has to find a way with the tools at hand.

Instead of a miscreant governor, the United States now has an unrepentant chief executive who treats the Department of Justice as his personal force. In 1962, the federal government would send marshals to Oxford. Today, when the lawbreaker is the commander in chief, the work falls to citizens: lawyers, nonprofits, preservation groups, and ordinary Americans who have taken this government to court again and again.

We are proud to join them. Nine members of my family—seven children and one grandchild of Robert Kennedy and one son of the late Senator Ted Kennedy—are seeking to join the litigation to stop construction of the triumphal arch that Donald Trump wants to build near Arlington National Cemetery, a sacred space for military veterans and their loved ones. The plaintiffs in the ongoing lawsuit include veterans, an architectural historian, the District of Columbia, and the Commonwealth of Virginia.

By building a gigantic memorial to himself, Trump would dishonor those who sacrificed themselves for this country. (His administration has claimed, variously, that the arch would honor the country’s 250th birthday, celebrate the troops, and serve as a military facility with snipers and drones.) The arch, modeled after the Arc de Triomphe, would be 250 feet high, more than double the height of every memorial in the capital except for the Washington Monument. Planned for a traffic circle next to the Potomac River, it would obstruct the view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that Congress has protected for generations of Americans. An eternal flame, which has burned for more than 60 years at President Kennedy’s grave, is bright enough to be seen by visitors at the Lincoln Memorial, but that too would be blocked. In the early morning, our parents’ resting place would lie in the shadow of the overbearing arch, as would many more graves. We should not allow this vanity to veil the sacrifice of the more than 400,000 men and women buried at Arlington.

Above all, building this arch is illegal. It violates two federal statutes: the Commemorative Works Act, which details a process for creating new memorials in D.C., as well as Title 40 of the U.S. Code, Section 8106, the law that forbids construction of any building or structure on federal reservations in Washington without the approval of Congress. Congress has given no such approval. The only path open to us in attempting to rein in the president is the courts.

That is why, after reading an article that illustrates how the arch would cast shadows deep into the cemetery, we decided to seek to intervene in the litigation against Trump and the National Park Service.

My mother liked to visit our father’s grave early in the morning, before going to Mass. She would head out of the house just after sunrise and drive herself down George Washington Memorial Parkway. Most of the guards came to know her white Oldsmobile by sight and would wave her through. She took great care in placing a simple wooden cross to mark his grave, and rough paving stones that reminded them both of the seaside streets of New England. She selected these words by my father to be cut into a granite block behind the grave:

It is from numberless diverse acts of courage and belief that human history is shaped. Each time a man stands up for an ideal, or acts to improve the lot of others, or strikes out against injustice, he sends forth a tiny ripple of hope, and crossing each other from a million different centers of energy and daring those ripples build a current that can sweep down the mightiest walls of oppression and resistance.

My mother passed away two years ago and is now buried beside her husband. People visiting their shared gravesite can read that quote and then, as I have done often, look up over the granite and down a hill once owned by Robert E. Lee. They can see Arlington Memorial Bridge leading to the Lincoln Memorial, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. addressed the crowds of the March on Washington. Their eyes can then trace the Reflecting Pool, the National Mall, the U.S. Capitol, and, finally, beyond that, the long-neglected neighborhoods on the southeast side of Washington, framed by the old site of RFK Stadium.

Arlington Memorial Bridge symbolized the rejoining of North and South after the Civil War. Each side faces the other across an unbroken line of sight. The view across the river connects two administrations separated by a century. President Kennedy’s grave is linked to the Lincoln Memorial just as his presidency, and the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts that followed, carried forward Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation and the amendments ending slavery. This visual connection, protected by law and tradition, will be broken if Trump succeeds in building his arch.

[Sebastian Smee: The arch is atrocious]

That view did not survive by accident. The beauty of Washington, D.C., derives in no small part from the vision of its architect, Pierre Charles L’Enfant. But we owe the longevity of its greatness in large measure to our past presidents and to Congress, including dedicated members of both parties who have overseen construction of every significant memorial in the District and guarded the central axis of the city.

More than a century ago, early plans for a bridge to Arlington from Washington called for triumphal arches. The McMillan Commission, whose members included the landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. and the sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, called the arches “unusually elaborate” and rejected them. “The broader and simpler the treatment of the bridge to Arlington,” the commission wrote, “the closer will be the connection” between the two shores.

Memorial Bridge was built according to that vision, aimed straight at the Lincoln Memorial, and the view has been preserved ever since. When construction finally began in 1926, the Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission’s report stated: “In order not to interfere with the view of the Lincoln Memorial as seen from Columbia Island, the bridge has been kept as low as possible consistent with sound engineering and economy.” Notably, officials did not build a pair of columns that Congress included when it passed the law creating the bridge. The Trump administration farcically claims that those columns give it Congress’s sign-off to build the arch now.

In 1986, to permanently safeguard the capital’s lasting character and dignity, Congress passed the Commemorative Works Act. The act requires that Congress specifically approve the construction of any new monument on federal land administered by the National Park Service or the General Services Administration—including where Trump proposes to build his arch. But Congress did not foresee a president who would flout the law, alongside a Justice Department that refuses to enforce even the most basic rules against him. President Trump has previously been reported to disrespect our nation’s fallen heroes. The arch would be yet another insult to the buried war dead. And that is why we stand now: to preserve the District of Columbia for every American and to preserve this hallowed ground. The national cemetery is this nation’s most sacred monument, where those who served rest in peace and honor. The laws Congress wrote were meant to protect it. They should be enforced.

title: Long Wave
summary: Ruth sets the children to dig for coins under the cushions of the ratty green sofa while she tries to get enough swimsuits and towels together. There is a big chest of drawers JP dragged home gleefully one evening, the scraping sound of her approaching, hollering for help. One of the other women, Sa...
content:
Ruth sets the children to dig for coins under the cushions of the ratty green sofa while she tries to get enough swimsuits and towels together. There is a big chest of drawers JP dragged home gleefully one evening, the scraping sound of her approaching, hollering for help. One of the other women, Sally, took it out into the concrete yard and sanded it down, repainted it, and then stenciled red flowers around the edges. As the women chopped carrots and argued about the rota, the children sneaked out at dusk and stuck their hands in the paint pot, left prints all over the front of the drawers. They get kids’ clothes from boxes on the street, charity sales and donations, and none of them fit right or they give way almost immediately at the seams but get shoved, nonetheless, into the chest of drawers and tugged out at random to put on whichever child needs them. Ori likes to go in by herself and dig thoughtfully through, chucking rejected dungarees and tie‑dye T‑shirts over her shoulder, plopping down on her backside to wrangle on leggings. Most of the swimsuits are nearly see-through from washing, the straps snapped, but Ruth manages to find enough and takes a handful of towels off the banister, puts them into the bag. The sun cream is out of date but will do the job.

When she gets back into the sitting room, the cushions have been heaved off the sofa and everyone is bouncing on the wheezing springs. They have uncovered crushed breadsticks and molding apple cores but also a handful of lost 20-pence pieces, just enough for them all to get into the lido if she lies about some of their ages. She has been working all week, but today she is in charge. Ori rushes over and burbles something about jumping as high as the trees like a bird—no, like a dragon—and then tugs a pirate hat down as far as it will fit onto Ruth’s head.

Let’s go, let’s go, she shouts, and everyone gathers, grabbing at shoes. There is Ori, who is 3—dressed this morning in a rainbow unicorn outfit with a wilting horn and a grubby tail—and Nora, with her shoes on the wrong feet, and Leo, who is 9 and an expert at making mayonnaise-and‑cheese sandwiches and wrapping them in foil. Last time they went to the lido he stole a rubber ring and he wears it slung around his middle now, hitching it up with one hand when it slithers down to his knees. There is also Bee, who is nearly 2 and who Ruth puts up on her hip to get out the door, and Tsembi, who is 7 and has a younger brother, Douglas, who bends to shit in his nappy beside the step, grunting intently.

Sally has been making planters out of pallets to try to make some more money and they are stacked up outside the house with for sale signs pinned to them. Ruth and the kids make it down to the path and go in a ragtag, snaky line away from the house, Ruth yelling hold hands, hold hands, until everyone is pinned to someone else and trailing along. There isn’t enough cash for the bus. They’ll walk. Ruth hitches Bee onto her shoulders and Leo and Tsembi take turns carrying Douglas. The walk takes a long time. She changes Douglas’s nappy while the others climb onto the back of a bus-stop bench and compare war wounds. Douglas’s shit is runny and filled with little white worms again. It won’t be long before the others get them too. Ori is yelling loudly about being the fastest, fastest, fastest one and twisting back and forth to show off her scrapes and bumps, her multiple Moomin Band-Aids, which are grubby and starting to peel. Leo is hanging near her, his fingers beginning to tap a little in the way they do when everything is too loud and busy, his eyes glazing; Ruth calls him closer, tries to distract him, asks him to pass her cloths and then take the dirty nappy to a bin. Nora and Ori are arguing about who can stand on the back of the bench the longest without holding on. Bee is crouching and prodding at a snail nearby while Tsembi shouts at her to give it a rest, he’s only little, give it a rest.

They make it to the pool. At the turnstile she counts heads and shoves the handful of coins in. They throw their towels down onto the brown grass and the kids strip their clothes off and fight over swimming costumes. She slathers sun cream on arms and legs and tries to stop Bee from falling in. Douglas examines his willy with his legs in the air and cries when a fat bee stings him on his round little belly. She scoops him up in one arm and gives him a sandwich. The older children are wading into the shallow end and lifting the water up in their hands and throwing it at one another, and Leo is dunking his head beneath the surface, where it must be good and quiet. Ori is leaping from the side over and over again, the force of her body leaving an after‑star‑shape in the air. Ruth gives Bee a sandwich too and puts on her own costume. It is one of JP’s and cuts in around the shoulders. Her mind is a rushing thing, trying to keep everyone in sight, tallying up who has sun cream on, thinking about what needs doing that day back at the house, thinking about the wood lice that have infested the room where she, JP, Leo, Nora and Ori sleep, which seem to dig their way up through the floors. There is a leak coming through the roof when it rains and sewage down the wall in the concrete yard whenever anyone upstairs flushes the chain.

One night she woke, damp with sweat. JP was beside her on the blow‑up mattress and Leo and Nora were sprawled across the single beds, but when she looked again, Ori was not there. Ruth went out into the corridor. There was noise from the rooms above, which are rented out separately by students whom they almost never see, only hear. She had a sudden damp nightmare vision of Ori being spirited away or, rather, having never existed—she had never had a child. Sometimes, when she was pregnant, she had wished her away and now she was gone, she had never even been. She ran down the stairs. The front door was swinging wide and there was a white square of mucky moon and streetlight across the floor. Someone—one of the students—had left a half‑finished wine bottle on the front step. Ori was not in the yard among the stacked, unsold planters and experimental wooden birdhouses. A noise from the sitting room. Cheerios crunched under her feet. Ori was bent over in the corner, drawing with an imaginary pencil on the floor, talking quietly to herself. When Ruth pressed gently on her spine she sagged into Ruth’s arms, closed her eyes. That was the first time she walked in her sleep.

The next day Ruth went and screamed at the hungover students, who came blearily out of their pizza-stinking rooms and scowled at her. Close the fucking front door, what is wrong with you?

Ruth tried everything to stop Ori from leaving the room at night. She tied her hands together by the wrists, she slept in front of the bedroom door, but always, somehow, Ori slipped free and Ruth would wake to her gone. It was a daytime and a nighttime problem. She was, JP said in exasperation after another desperate loudspeaker callout in the supermarket, a runner. Where had she gotten it from? This speedy, goat-like need to escape? Often, at the point of realizing she was lost, she would sit and wail. When they found her, she would be beside herself: You lost me, where were you?

Ruth found herself thinking of the nights when the door of her childhood bedroom was locked against escape and she would knock on the walls and it would mean, I am here, I am here, are you there? One breakfast she undid the tie from JP’s dressing gown and rummaged around in the cupboard. The children were at the table, spoons hovering over their porridge, rumpled from sleep, watching her with suspicion. Ruth dug out a saucepan lid and tied it around Ori’s neck, gave her a metal spoon to bash it with. Ori’s eyes grew wide and she stood up on her chair. Bang, bang, bang, went the spoon on the saucepan, bang, bang, bang.

That’s loud, JP said, holding closed her dressing gown.

Well, we can hear where she is now, at least in the day, Ruth said.

After that, Ori would often be given the saucepan lid or, if there was nothing else, stones from the ground or two sticks broken off a tree. JP started calling her Oystercatcher after the birds that hammer mussels and clams to try to get them open.

At night, though, the sleepwalking continued and then began to get worse. On one bad occasion, Ori had made it all the way to the garden and was fiddling with the gate that led to the road when Ruth got to her. Ori was barefoot and tangle‑haired, moving fast. Ruth grabbed her, took her back inside, held her. Everyone was awake now, a bit upset, shifting around, Nora complaining, Leo singing quietly and tapping his fingers. Ruth, to try to calm them, began to tell the story of the knocking, not the wall one but the other. When you were in my belly, she said to Ori, I knocked and said, Hello, hello, and from the other side you knocked and said, I hear you, hello, how are you today?

JP went out of the room and came back with the saucepan lid. She strung it—more, Ruth suspected, for comedic effect than anything else—around Ori’s neck, tied a wooden spoon to the edge of the lid. Just knock in your sleep, she said, and Nora and Leo howled and danced around, pretending to be sleepwalking, while Ori frowned thoughtfully, working out whether to be annoyed.

Later, Ruth woke hard. A noise had come into her dreams and disturbed them. She had been dreaming about her mother in the kitchen of the house, she was wearing a green apron and stirring something in a large metal bowl and then she turned and looked straight at Ruth and said: Is someone at the door again? Ruth sat up. JP was already out of bed, crossing the room. She opened the door into the corridor. Past her Ruth could see Ori. She was sitting on the floor, cross‑legged, head bobbing to the sound as she struck the saucepan lid over and over and over.

I hear you, JP said, I hear you, you’re here, don’t wake the whole house.

She takes the younger children into the water, floating them on their backs. She knows some of the other parents there a little; she also sees a few childminders with their own hordes of children, some serious swimmers in the main lanes plowing up and down, up and down. Leo gets Ori on his shoulders and ducks beneath the water and then explodes upward and she spins backwards and lands with a muffled boom and they do it again. Nora wants to show Ruth every one of the drowning beetles and wasps she is rescuing from the water. Douglas is mostly scared and clings on to her back like a splatted, soggy thing. They stay in for a few hours and then crawl out and lie on the grass under the sun. Some of the kids cry because they are tired and hungry. She feeds them sandwiches and they count out their coins and there are just enough for chips from the van. Leo comes back with a container and some ketchup. Ruth wraps Bee and Douglas and Ori in towels and lies down among them and sings them a song and they doze and wake and cry a bit and wipe their snotty noses on her arms and then sleep again. Ruth thinks Ori is sleeping but feels something on her cheeks and when she opens her eyes Ori’s face is directly above hers, nose to nose, water droplets falling from the strands of her straggly hair. Another of the women had given the kids haircuts, one after the other, bang, bang, bang, army‑style, and they are all bowl‑cutted now, spiky around the edges.

Mama, come, Ori says, come on, Mama, up.

She unravels herself from the other two and gets up and takes Ori’s hand. Leo is reading a book he has stolen from a sunbathing woman’s blanket. Tsembi is swimming a choppy doggy‑paddle up and down, copying the lane swimmers. Nora is digging for worms. Ori and Ruth investigate the bushes around the edge of the pool. There is a stretch of rubber tiles and an old, broken sprinkler system with rusted, sharp edges, and beyond that some giant overgrown wisteria. Ori has brought some worn plastic animals without Ruth noticing, a zebra with barely any stripes left, a polar bear without back legs.

What do bears eat? Ori says, shoving the nose of the polar bear into the hardened ground.

I don’t know. Honey?

No. Silly Mama. Definitely not.

I don’t know, then.

Maybe fish?

Yeah, maybe.

Here’s a bear dance I just made up, she says, and jiggles and jaggles around, pushing her belly and her lips out and then sucking them in, sticking out her bottom.

That’s cool, I like it.

Yeah, maybe. Now you do it.

Ruth tries to copy the dance exactly, waggling around. Not bad? she says.

A bit bad, Ori says. A bit poo‑poo. She laughs and laughs.

JP comes down after work and kicks off her shoes and sticks her feet in the pool. Ori flings her arms around JP’s neck and Nora and Leo show her the handstands they have been perfecting in the pool. The little ones have woken up and are back in the water.

How’s it going? Ruth says to JP.

Bouncing and bouncing and bouncing, JP says, bouncing motherfuckers, they need to stop bouncing and get a job. How’s it going in the madhouse?

Fine, Ruth says, and tells her about worms and nappies.

I’m so tired that I could sink into the water and sleep there, actually.

Like a whale, JP says. Do you want to do a lap?

Yeah, Ruth says.

She leaves the children and goes to the adult side of the swimming pool. Her swimming costume is so thin, she thinks maybe everyone can see her bottom through it. She drops into the water. Some of the other women are wearing goggles and swim hats. She lets herself go down under the surface. It is not silent there but the noise comes wonky through the water and resounds bubbling through her. She swims along the floor with her belly scraping and then rises up and does a couple of lengths and then goes back to JP, who is yelling at Bee not to touch Douglas’s bottom if he tells her not to. She can tell, from looking at Leo, that he is overwhelmed by the noise and the argument. She sits beside him until he seems better and then she and JP lie in the last bit of the sun. The warmth feels good on Ruth’s closed eyelids.

Look, JP says. When Ruth opens her eyes, JP is up on her elbows. Ruth levers herself upright. The children are playing a game. She hasn’t seen them play this one before.

What is it? she says.

Have you not seen this yet? Just watch.

Nora has blindfolded herself with a towel wrapped around her head. All the children are there, on the grassy bit a little away from the pool, but Douglas isn’t really playing. They all have two stones, including Nora, whose stones are a little bigger than everyone else’s. They space themselves out. Blindfolded, Nora knocks her two stones against each other, tap, tap. The rest of them tap their stones together and Nora lurches forward, already laughing without making noise, and tries to get to them by figuring out where their taps came from. She nearly gets Leo because he is laughing so hard, but he skips out of the way and Nora has to stop and knock her stones together again. The rest of them, standing still, knock their stones together and the sound means: I am here. Nora comes for them. Ori darts away and then climbs up the metal fence and Nora knocks her stones together, asking, Where are you, where are you, and Ori knocks her stones together from the fence, I am here, I am here, and Nora comes and catches at her feet. They play for a long time, taking turns with the blindfold.

A knocking game, Ruth says.

Isn’t it good? Ori came up with it yesterday in the garden when I locked them out so I could make dinner. We should go, JP says.

Yup, she says.

They walk home the long way, carrying all of the children’s shoes in their hands. The children play a game involving trains chugging along a track. They stop briefly at a playground with a rusty red swing and a dirt groove beneath. The others like the slide, going down in a pile, seeing who can run down, but Ori likes the swing. She will stay on the swing for hours if they let her, clinging on to the metal chains, her torso tipped backwards, her chin rolled to the sky. JP and Ruth sit on a bench and talk about the child-care funding they had hoped was going to help them out but is less than half of what they thought it was going to be and whether they think the homeschooling is going okay. They talk about these things a lot and sometimes there are meetings in the house with the other women and with new women who come and go and mostly they all say: I don’t know what to do, I’m not sure. Sometimes the meetings are really good and people cry and talk and sometimes they all get annoyed and impatient and no one agrees and they just argue until they’re too tired to continue. Another meeting is scheduled for later that night after the kids are asleep. JP rolls her eyes and sticks out her tongue and says, I can’t talk about Sally quitting her job and making birdhouses anymore, she’s already bringing in hardly anything, and Douglas and Tsembi eat so much.

Ruth laughs. Then they talk about what they want to say tonight.

This is what I was going to say, shall I try it out on you? JP says.

Go for it, Ruth says.

Great. Hold on, she says, and they check on the children, count them, and Ruth looks for Leo, who listens to everything, and makes sure he is not close-up. Let’s go, everyone, they shout. They walk together along the road and JP holds Ruth’s hand.

Well, I was going to say that I love them, obviously. I love all of them. I love Leo and Nora and I feel that I am the most lucky person to be their mum. I love Ori, I love that kid, did you know that?

Yeah, Ruth says.

I love their weird bodies and their silly sentences and I love that they were tiny and useless and now they’re just these crazy roommates. I was going to say all that but then I was going to say: I love them but I hate them.

Oh yeah, that’s true, Ruth says.

Like, what have they done to my life? Do they know that they are little bombs hidden under my floors and that they go off 10 times a day?

Fifty times.

A hundred and a thousand and a million times. They don’t know who I was before. I was a whole person. I was a child once and then I had a child and that child killed the child I was. That is insane.

It’s insane.

I was going to say something like that, JP says. What do you think?

I think it sounds good, Ruth says. I think I’m going to say something like that too.

title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
summary: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face lega...
content:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

content:

  • Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria

An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
summary: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and humanThe relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue...
content:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

content:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
